items.title: Eyewitness memories can be planted
items.claim: Elizabeth Loftus's lab implanted entirely false childhood memories in adult participants. What proportion came to believe the fake event was real?
items.reveal_title: About a quarter of people 'remembered' something that never happened
items.reveal:
In the 'Lost in the Mall' study (Loftus & Pickrell, 1995), 25% of participants came to recall a fabricated childhood event after being told by a family member it had occurred.

Later work with more vivid scenarios reached implantation rates around 50%.
items.why: Memory feels like recording. It is reconstruction, and reconstruction is suggestible.

items.title: Phineas Gage's recovery
items.claim: In 1848 an iron rod passed through the frontal lobe of railroad worker Phineas Gage. He survived. How long did he live afterwards?
items.reveal_title: Gage lived for roughly 12 more years
items.reveal:
Gage died in 1860 after epileptic seizures. Recent scholarship (Macmillan, 2000) suggests his personality changes were less extreme and more temporary than the textbook caricature implies.

He worked as a stagecoach driver in Chile in his later years.
items.why: Famous case studies are often simplified in retelling. Lesion evidence is more nuanced than the headline.
